title: "Fiction Is Not Counterfactual"
abstract: |
  Does a story that never says how many hairs Holmes had, or how a tossed coin landed, nonetheless make one answer true? Blumberg and Holguín have recently argued that it does. Our attitudes toward the questions a fiction leaves open (we can wonder, hope and assign probabilities, but cannot know) are what we should expect if there are facts we are ignorant of, and the facts can be located: what is true in a fiction is what would be true if its settled claims were true, on a Stalnakerian semantics for counterfactuals. I argue that fiction and counterfactuals come apart exactly where this principle needs them to agree. Strengthen the antecedent of a counterfactual with a detail that bears on a chancy outcome and the outcome can change; add the same detail to a story without settling the outcome, and it does not. Saving the principle requires a rule for fiction that counterfactuals reject. A semantics on which fictional claims are evaluated against the information a story provides, weighted by a Reality Principle for credence, predicts both the attitudes and the asymmetry, with no single world. What remains of the case for one is the preference for bivalence.

# Lewis's question {#sec-intro}

When Holmes first meets Watson, does he have an odd or an even number of hairs on his head? Lewis thought it "absurd to suppose" that such questions "about the world of Sherlock Holmes have answers" [@Lewis1978, 42]. Blumberg and Holguín [-@BlumbergHolguin2025] argue that Lewis was wrong: "for any given work of fiction, there is a single world that determines what's true in it, and that world is as rich in detail as reality itself" (176). The parity of Holmes's hairs is "as factual as the question of whether he is a detective" (151). We just cannot know it.

Their case has two parts. The first is a profile of attitudes. We can wonder whether the coin tossed in the last scene of a television series landed heads. We can think a biased coin more likely than not to have landed heads, and we can hope it did. But we cannot know, or be sure, how it landed. Blumberg and Holguín (hereafter B&H) argue that this profile is what we should expect if there is a fact of which we are ignorant. The second part locates the fact. By their PRINCIPAL REALITY PRINCIPLE (PRP), what is true in a fiction is what would be true if the fiction's settled claims were true, on Stalnaker's semantics for counterfactuals. Fictional truth is counterfactual truth. B&H support the identification by showing that indeterminate counterfactuals display the same attitude profile as indeterminate fiction.

B&H consider the option I will defend, that there being "no fact of the matter" about whether p "is perfectly compatible with one's rationally having opinions about p, wondering whether p, and so on" (167), and credit Khoo [-@Khoo2022] with a related line about counterfactuals (167 n. 33). They set it aside because of arguments from embedding patterns, which they say drive their case more than the PRP does (183 n. 53). I answer those arguments. But my main argument is new: fiction and counterfactuals come apart, and in the place where the PRP needs them to agree.

Strengthen the antecedent of a counterfactual with a detail that bears on a chancy outcome, and the outcome can change. Add the same detail to a story, without settling the outcome, and the outcome does not change; it stays open. Suppose a reunion special for the series had revealed that a sudden gust caught the coin as it was tossed, and still not shown how it landed. Compare:

(A) It's about even odds that, if there had been no gust, the coin would have landed the other way.

(B) It's about even odds that, if the writers had left the special out, the coin would have landed differently.

I predict that (A) will be judged fine and (B) absurd (@sec-test says how to check). On the PRP they stand or fall together.

I defend three claims. First, *the strengthening test refutes the PRP as B&H state it*, and every way of saving it adds a rule for fiction that counterfactuals reject (@sec-test, @sec-remains). Second, *a story-state semantics passes the test*. On this semantics, bare fictional claims and attitudes toward them are evaluated against the information a work provides, weighted by a Reality Principle for credence. It predicts B&H's attitude profile and their embedding data with no single world, and given two bridge principles it agrees with them on every attitude toward a single fiction (@sec-states). Third, *what remains of the single world is a preference for bivalence*, bought with facts whose grounds B&H concede will often be "almost entirely arbitrary" (188).

The alternative is not new in spirit. Williams and Woodward [-@WilliamsWoodward2021] argued that the right attitude toward what a fiction leaves open is an imaginative credence that should "match the conditional probability of p given the fictive evidence", and that "there are, so to speak, no fictional facts of the matter". Lewis's own analyses of truth in fiction let a story's truths grow with the story [@Lewis1978], and Badura and Berto [-@BaduraBerto2019] model truth in fiction as belief revision. Oppy and Raivars [-@OppyRaivars2026] and Khoo [-@Khoo2026] reply to B&H by contesting their data. My contribution is the strengthening test, which separates the views where attitudes toward a single fiction cannot, together with a semantics precise enough to show that the alternative passes it.

# The case for fictional reality {#sec-bh}

B&H work within the modal approach to truth in fiction. A bare internal claim, such as "Holmes lives on Baker Street" on its natural reading, carries a silent operator $\square_f$. It is true iff its prejacent holds at every world in a set $\mathrm{Fic}_f$. The *principal truths* of $f$ are the fictional claims that can, at least in principle, be known to be true in $f$ (156): what the work states or depicts, what its author intended, and what follows from these against background reality. P-Fic$_f$ is the set of worlds compatible with them. The *standard analysis* sets $\mathrm{Fic}_f$ = P-Fic$_f$. On it, a claim the principal truths leave unsettled is false, and so is its negation.

B&H's central case is the last episode of *JAG*. Bud tosses a fair coin to decide which of Mac and Harm will resign and follow the other, and the series ends with the coin in the air. B&H stipulate, "perhaps counterfactually", that the writers had no intentions about the outcome "and then never thought about the events of JAG again" (161).^[In 2019 *NCIS: Los Angeles* brought Harm and Mac back. According to recaps, Mac had won the toss and Harm had passed up a JAG post in London to join her in San Diego [@Hurley2019; @Mitovich2019], which is tails on B&H's labelling (161). B&H's note 26 cites, as evidence that no one knows how the coin landed, a piece announcing that the sequel "will finally reveal who won the coin flip" [@Stein2019]; it is dated a week before the reveal aired. Like B&H, I set this aside. My test in @sec-test uses a hypothetical special because the actual sequel settles the question.] With the complement "Bud's coin landed heads", they report that *know*, *be sure* and *know whether* are unacceptable; *think* is unacceptable for a fair coin and acceptable for a coin biased 2:1, and *doubt* likewise; "It's .5 likely that" is acceptable; *wonder whether* is acceptable; *wish* is unacceptable; *hope* is acceptable (161–167).

The standard analysis predicts otherwise. Anyone who knows the show knows that "Bud's coin landed heads" is not a principal truth, so on the standard analysis they know it is false. Frege puzzles aside, the analysis therefore validates ATTITUDE EQUIVALENCE: one's attitudes toward a fictional claim's being true in $f$ are one's attitudes toward its being a principal truth (167). So the informed viewer should know whether the coin landed heads, be sure it did not, and be able to wish it had. Treating indeterminate claims as undefined does no better. A known gap makes "I wonder whether the King of France is happy" bad, while known fictional indeterminacy does not make "I wonder whether Bud's coin landed heads" bad (169–171). And B&H argue that any trivalent view predicts that "I know whether p is true, but I don't know whether p" can be uttered truly (171).

B&H then argue from embedding patterns to a single world. They find this inference "unimpeachable" (172): "I don't know that Bud's coin landed heads. And I don't know that it failed to land heads. So I don't know whether Bud's coin landed heads." Since "fail to" lexicalises negation, the inference requires SCOPELESSNESS: $\neg\square_f p$ iff $\square_f\neg p$ (173). Because $\square_f$ quantifies over $\mathrm{Fic}_f$, Scopelessness forces $\mathrm{Fic}_f$ to be a singleton (175 n. 39), and fictional excluded middle (FEM) follows: $\square_f p \vee \square_f \neg p$ (176 n. 40). The second pattern is a fictional analogue of Higginbotham's [-@Higginbotham1986] quantified conditionals. "Every character in The Breakfast Club failed the test" and "No character in The Breakfast Club passed the test" are equivalent, even with the quantifier taking scope outside the fiction operator. "If FEM is invalid," B&H say, "then it's unclear how this is to be explained" (181).

Finally, the PRP locates the world: $\square_{f,w}\, p$ iff P-Fic$_{f,w} > p$ is true at $w$, with $>$ Stalnaker's conditional [@Stalnaker1968] (182). The world of $f$ is "the unique world that would accurately represent how things are, were all the principal claims of f really true" (183). Indeterminate counterfactuals, such as "If Flippy had been flipped, it would have landed heads", show the same attitude profile as fiction. B&H take this as "strong abductive support" for the PRP (182): "we see no better way of explaining these similarities" (183). Since similarity rarely favours one candidate world over another, the selection function picks "at random, so to speak" (184), following the views of arbitrary selection defended by Hawthorne [-@Hawthorne2005], Schulz [-@Schulz2017] and Bacon [-@Bacon2015] (184 n. 55). That is why, unless one has "the word of an oracle, say", one's evidence "won't be able to rule out any of the possible results" (184).

# The strengthening test {#sec-test}

## Counterfactuals

Any adequate theory of counterfactuals must respect two judgements about chancy outcomes. Suppose a fair coin was tossed and landed heads.

1. *Relevant strengthening can change the outcome.* "Had the coin been tossed in a gust of wind, it would still have landed heads" is not true. Where a coin lands depends sensitively on the conditions of the toss.
2. *Irrelevant strengthening cannot.* "Had a moth been fluttering in the next room, the coin would still have landed heads" is fine. Cases like Morgenbesser's coin suggest that "only match among those facts causally independent of the antecedent should count towards similarity" [@Schaffer2004, 305].

A Stalnakerian can respect both. Order worlds by similarity to actuality, and break the many near-ties by agreement with one fixed assignment of values to the exogenous variables of the apt causal model, the same assignment for every antecedent. A gust is a cause of the landing, so strengthening by a gust redraws the coin. The moth is not, so it leaves the coin alone. This is the best the PRP can do, because the PRP evaluates fiction with the very function that evaluates counterfactuals. If a selection function of this kind fails the test below, the PRP fails it.

## The case

Suppose that, years after *JAG* ended, its makers produced a reunion special set in the minutes before the finale's last scene. In it we see that a sudden gust caught the coin as Bud tossed it. We still never see how it lands, and, as in B&H's stipulation, the makers have no view about it. The special is consistent with everything in *JAG*. So its principal content, call it $B$, is a subset of *JAG*'s, call it $A$. Asked about the series as it now stands, I predict that an informed viewer will judge as follows:

| | | PRP | Story state |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | It's about even odds that, if there had been no gust, the coin would have landed the other way. | ✓ | ✓ |
| (B) | It's about even odds that, if the writers had left the special out, the coin would have landed differently. | ✓ | ✗ |
| (C) | If the special had shown the coin landing heads, it would have landed heads. | ✓ | ✓ |
| (D) | It's about even odds that, if the writers had left the special out, the coin would have landed heads. | ✓ | ✓ |

: Predicted judgements, ✓ (acceptable) or ✗ (unacceptable), for the gust case. {#tbl-test}

My own judgements are (A) ✓, (B) ✗, (C) ✓ and (D) ✓. They are predictions, to be tested, not reported data.^[A design: cross the locus of the antecedent (the gust versus the telling) with relevance (a detail bearing on the coin, such as the gust, versus one that does not, such as a scene of Bud's childhood), and elicit probabilities rather than acceptability. The crux is the contrast between the two telling conditions. The PRP with causal tie-breaking predicts about .5 when the omitted detail is relevant and about 0 when it is irrelevant; the story-state view predicts about 0 for both. Two further probes are needed. Viewers may assume the makers decided how the coin landed, so ask "Had the makers decided how the coin landed?" and analyse by answer. And a variant in which the gust makes heads nine times as likely as tails separates the treatment of cross-telling comparisons in @sec-states from simple anchoring. Mixtures matter: a mean of .5 for (B) could hide a population of 0s and 1s.]

(B) and (D) share an antecedent and a frame, a credence report on a counterfactual about the telling with a bare fictional consequent, and differ only in the consequent. (D) shows that speakers give that consequent the reading B&H's credence data require, on which it can be .5 likely; a reading on which it concerns what the story settles would make (D) absurd. (C) shows that the bare consequent follows the counterfactual telling. So the rejection of (B) is not a retreat to a "what the story says" reading. (A) and (B) then differ only in whether the antecedent removes the gust from the story's events or the special from its telling.

## What the PRP predicts

Under the PRP, the world of the series as it now stands is $s(B, @)$, the closest world to actuality at which everything in *JAG* and the special holds. Had the special been left out, the world of the series would have been $s(A, w')$, where $w'$ is the closest world at which the writers did not make the special. I assume that $s(A, w') = s(A, @)$. The special's absence does not alter which worlds are most like actuality in respects bearing on Bud's coin. Dropping the assumption only adds a further source of difference.

Is $s(A, @)$ a world in which a gust catches the coin? Similarity to actuality is silent, since there is no actual toss to match. But by any link between selection and chance of the kind B&H need (@sec-states), an agent's credence that the selection lands on a gust-world equals the in-story chance of a gust at that moment, which is small. So almost certainly $s(A, @) \notin B$, and $s(B, @) \neq s(A, @)$. The two worlds differ in a cause of the coin's landing. That is exactly the difference that, by judgement 1, redraws the coin. Whatever tie-breaking gets (A) right, by letting the landing depend on the gust, makes $s(A, @)$ and $s(B, @)$ disagree about the landing about half the time. So the PRP predicts (B) ✓, just as it predicts (D) ✓.

Could a defender of the PRP keep (B) false by evaluating the bare consequent at the actual series' world whatever the counterfactual says about the telling? Then (C) fails. Had the special shown heads, the coin would have landed heads only if it does at $s(B, @)$, and that is even odds.

The general point is this. The PRP makes adding a detail to a story the same operation as strengthening the antecedent of a counterfactual. For details that bear on an open chancy question, strengthening a counterfactual's antecedent can change the answer, and adding the detail to a story does not. No selection function that gets the counterfactuals right gets the fiction right.

## Why not time?

The contrast could be posed over time: did the special change how the coin landed? But B&H have an answer to that. On one of their options for fictional change, ordinary talk "is directed at the final version"; on the other, by default "we talk about what's true in the most recent version" (193–194). Either way, claims made before and after the special are assessed at one world. Developed as relativism about assessment [@McGonigal2013], this gets temporal judgements right. B&H, like the literature on serial fiction [@McGonigal2013; @Caplan2014; @Lee2024], discuss change that revises; their defaults apply all the more to a special that only adds. Counterfactuals about the telling are not so absorbed, because they change which version is final.

# Story states {#sec-states}

## The fragment

The rival view evaluates bare fictional claims against a body of information shifted by the story.

1. *Priors.* For each world $w$, $\pi_w$ is a probability over worlds that encodes $w$'s regularities, together with the chances internal to whatever is supposed. It is a Reality Principle of the kind Lewis [-@Lewis1978] and Walton [-@Walton1990] proposed for truth in fiction (as B&H note, 182 n. 51), applied to credence rather than to truth.
2. *Shift.* $P_f(w)$ is the set of worlds compatible with $f$'s principal truths as they stand at $w$. For an information state $s$ with credence $C$:
   - $s \oplus f = \bigcup_{w \in s} \mathrm{supp}\, \pi_w(\cdot \mid P_f(w))$;
   - $C \oplus f = \sum_w C(w)\, \pi_w(\cdot \mid P_f(w))$.
3. *Bare claims.* A bare declarative $\varphi$ is interpreted inside the shift, with its connectives, its embedded counterfactuals, and any quantifiers inside the fiction. Here $|\varphi|$ is the ordinary content of $\varphi$.
   - $s$ *supports* $f{:}\varphi$ iff $s \oplus f \subseteq |\varphi|$.
   - $s$ *rejects* $f{:}\varphi$ iff $s \oplus f \cap |\varphi| = \varnothing$.
   - Counterfactuals inside $\varphi$ get their ordinary semantics at each world of $s \oplus f$.
   - A quantifier outside the fiction binds into it pointwise: $\forall x\, f{:}\varphi(x)$ is supported iff $f{:}\varphi(a)$ is supported for every $a$, and rejected iff $f{:}\varphi(a)$ is rejected for some $a$.
4. *Tellings.* A counterfactual about the telling shifts the story parameter: its bare consequent is evaluated against the story as it would then have been. Where the consequent is anaphoric on the actual telling ("differently", "still", "the other way"), the anaphor is resolved by mapping each candidate world of the actual telling to its nearest candidates in the counterfactual telling.
5. *Truth.* Internal "true" is transparent: $f{:}(\varphi \text{ is true}) \equiv f{:}\varphi$. A bare claim about $f$ is *right* at $w$, as assessed from a context $c$, iff $\{w\} \oplus f$ supports it, with $f$ taken as it stands at $w$ at the time of $c$.
6. *Attitudes.* The story is a parameter of the context, not an operator inside the complement. An attitude verb applies its ordinary entry to the subject's own state shifted by $f$: $D_S \oplus f$ for her certainties and $C_S \oplus f$ for her credences.

Five consequences matter.

**Scopelessness without a world.** Because $\oplus$ distributes over unions, support and rejection are settled world by world. So $f{:}\varphi$ behaves like a homogeneous plural predication. Like "The children are asleep", it is supported when every candidate world is a $\varphi$-world, rejected when none is, and otherwise neither [@Kriz2019]. "Bud's coin didn't land heads" and "Bud's coin failed to land heads" both express $f{:}\neg h$, which is supported exactly when $f{:}h$ is rejected. That is Scopelessness, and the inference B&H call unimpeachable is valid. In B&H's derivation of a single world (175 n. 39), "not every world in Fic$_f$ is a p-world" is a fact about the state: the story does not settle $p$. It is not the content of any bare claim, so the slide from two candidate worlds to a falsified Scopelessness never starts.

**Excluded middle.** $f{:}(h \vee \neg h)$ is supported, and with transparent truth so is "Either 'the coin landed heads' is true or 'the coin landed tails' is true". But neither $f{:}h$ nor $f{:}\neg h$ is supported, so FEM, read as a claim about what the story makes so, fails.

**The Higginbotham pattern.** On B&H's mixed reading, "No character in The Breakfast Club passed the test" says of every character $x$ that it is not the case that, in the film, $x$ passed, and "Every character in The Breakfast Club failed the test" says of every character $x$ that, in the film, $x$ did not pass (their (43)). Negation of a homogeneous claim swaps support and rejection. So for each $x$ the two open sentences are supported together and rejected together, and by the clause for quantifying in, so are the two quantified claims. Von Fintel's [-@vonFintel1997, 33] proposal that bare conditionals carry a homogeneity presupposition, so that they "obey the Excluded Middle", would explain Higginbotham's conditional equivalence in the same way. FEM is not needed to explain the equivalence.

**Refinement.** If $Y$'s principal content includes $X$'s, then $s \oplus Y \subseteq s \oplus X$. So nothing $X$ supports or rejects becomes unsettled in $Y$, and given the assessment clause no bare claim goes from right to wrong without a revision. This parallels MacFarlane's [-@MacFarlane2003] treatment of future contingents, on which an utterance that is neither true nor false as assessed from the moment it is made can be true as assessed from a later one. B&H's view, with one selected world per stage, is the fictional counterpart of the "thin red line", which MacFarlane, "like Belnap and Green" [-@BelnapGreen1994], takes to amount to "giving up objective indeterminism" (325). Only the support half of Refinement holds. $C \oplus Y$ is an image of $C$, not $C \oplus X$ conditioned, and nothing below needs more.

**The attitude table.** For a viewer who knows *JAG*, $D \oplus f$ contains heads-worlds and tails-worlds, and $C \oplus f$ gives each .5 (2/3 and 1/3 for the biased coin).
- *Know*, *be sure* and *know whether*, which require support in $D \oplus f$, are unacceptable.
- "It's .5 likely" is acceptable.
- *Think*, which B&H gloss as finding something "more likely than not" (175), is unacceptable for the fair coin and acceptable for the biased one, and *doubt* likewise.
- *Wonder* and *hope*, which require the question to be open in $D \oplus f$, are acceptable.
- *Wish*, which requires $\neg h$ to be supported, is unacceptable.

No verb needs a special projection rule: each keeps its lexical entry, and all of them look at the same shifted state.^[Blumberg and Strohminger [-@BlumbergStrohminger2025, §4.1] observe that "Bill believes that Juliet died, but he hopes that she survived" is infelicitous, which fits a view on which hope toward a story is constrained by the same state as belief about it.]

## The test

In words, the story-state view treats a story as a body of information. Adding a detail to a story discards some of the ways things might be and moves none of them. A counterfactual, by contrast, moves from a way things are to another way things might have been.

- **(A)** For each candidate world of the series as it stands, the counterfactual "if there had been no gust, the coin would have landed the other way" is evaluated at that world. With a chancy coin it holds at about half of them, so (A) is ✓. (Here I grant B&H a Stalnakerian semantics for counterfactuals, with chances guiding credence about selection.)
- **(D)** The consequent is evaluated against *JAG* without the special. The coin lands heads at about half of its candidate worlds, so (D) is ✓.
- **(C)** In the counterfactual telling, the coin lands heads at every candidate world, so (C) is ✓.
- **(B)** "Differently" is anaphoric on the actual telling. Each candidate world of the series as it stands is mapped to its nearest candidates in *JAG* without the special. By Refinement, every candidate of the longer telling is already a candidate of the shorter one, so the nearest candidate to each world is that world itself. At every pair the coin lands one way, once. So "the coin would have landed differently" is rejected, and (B) is ✗.^[For a detail that shifts in-story chances, such as a gust that makes heads nine times as likely, the map should be the coupling of the two candidate measures that makes the outcomes agree as far as their chances allow. That coupling coincides with the identity when the chances are unchanged. It then predicts a probability of .4 that the coin would have landed differently, the least disagreement the change in chances permits, and it leaves (D) at .5.]

The PRP cannot reproduce this. It has one world for each telling, and the world for the shorter telling, $s(A, @)$, is not the world for the longer one. The map from the actual telling's world to the counterfactual telling's world is then a map between two different worlds that differ in a cause of the landing.

## Gaps without vagueness

The view has truth-value gaps, so B&H's objection to trivalent views (171) applies to it. With a transparent internal truth predicate, "I know whether p is true, but I don't know whether p" is on its bare reading a contradiction, so it is bad, as B&H say. It is acceptable only when "true" is heard as "true according to the story", and then it should be: "I know whether it's true in *JAG* that the coin landed heads (it isn't), but I don't know whether the coin landed heads."

The gaps are not those of vagueness either. B&H distinguish fictional from vague indeterminacy because vague claims are bad under attitudes and invite "Yes and no" (185–187). In a story state, the candidate worlds are not precisifications of "heads". They are factual alternatives, weighted by chances, which the story leaves open. So *wonder* and *hope* are licensed, and "Yes and no" is not; the right answer is "the story doesn't say". The indeterminacy is neither semantic, nor metaphysical, nor ignorance of a hidden fact. It is the incompleteness of the information a work provides, which was Lewis's view, made fit for attitudes.

## Absorption

On B&H's view, a credence that $p$ is true in $f$ is a credence about where the selection lands. B&H need such credences to track in-story chances; they suggest that a rational agent "will be doxastically indifferent to the various possibilities compatible with the principal truths" (175), while granting that they lack "a direct argument" that credence has the needed structure. Two bridge principles make the suggestion precise. Both are my strengthenings of it.

- **Chance–selection link.** Given any world $w$, $S$'s credence that $s(P_f(w), w)$ lies in $X$ is $\pi_w(X \mid P_f(w))$.
- **Openness.** The selections that $S$'s certainties leave open, given $w$, are exactly the support of $\pi_w(\cdot \mid P_f(w))$. This is B&H's own claim that, without an oracle, evidence cannot "rule out any of the possible results" (184), together with the assumption that $\pi_w$ gives positive weight to every possible result.

Given both, for every attitude in B&H's table and any single fiction, $S$ bears the attitude to $\square_f \varphi$ on B&H's view iff she bears it to $f{:}\varphi$ on the story-state view.^[For credence, average the selection over the link: $C_S(\square_f \varphi) = \sum_w C_S(w)\, \pi_w(|\varphi| \mid P_f(w)) = (C_S \oplus f)(|\varphi|)$. This is a version of Lewis's [-@Lewis1976] result that credence in a Stalnaker conditional is credence imaged on its antecedent. For certainty, Openness gives: $S$ is sure of $\square_f \varphi$ iff every open selection is a $\varphi$-world iff $D_S \oplus f \subseteq |\varphi|$. The other attitudes in the table are defined from these.] So the data in B&H's §6 cannot decide between the views. Nor can the counterfactual parallel of their §9, since any view on which these attitudes are evaluated against a shifted state predicts it. Absorption fixes credences one story at a time, and says nothing about how the selections for two stories are related. That is why the strengthening test, which compares two tellings, can do what attitudes toward a single fiction cannot.

# What remains of the single world {#sec-remains}

The strengthening test refutes the PRP as B&H state it: fictional truth as counterfactual truth at the actual world, under the selection function counterfactuals use. It does not refute every single-world view. There are three ways to keep a single world, and each passes the test.

**Anchoring.** Let the selection function vary with context, as Stalnaker allows, so that whenever two tellings are under discussion, the world of the shorter one is chosen inside the longer. The shorter telling then gets the longer telling's world, and (B) is ✗. But this cannot be a general rule for counterfactuals. Applied to the toss itself, it would require that whenever "if the coin had been tossed" and "if it had been tossed in a gust" are discussed together, the first select a gust-world. Then "Had the coin been tossed, it would have landed heads, but had it been tossed in a gust, it might have landed tails" would come out contradictory, though it states precisely the sensitivity that judgement 1 records. So anchoring is a rule for fiction alone. It also differs in prediction from the story-state view. With "still", the anaphor on the actual telling licenses "If the writers had left the special out, there would still have been a gust". Without it, "If the writers had left the special out, there would have been a gust" is unsupported. Anchoring makes both true.

**Defaults.** Fix one assignment of values to the exogenous variables of every story, or rank the questions a world answers and fix a default answer to each. Then let the world of $f$ be the P-Fic$_f$-world that best matches the defaults. Rank the landing above the gust, and the special leaves the landing alone. But actuality supplies no values for the variables of merely possible coins, so the defaults are not similarity to actuality. They are a stipulated default world for possibilia. An ordering that keeps outcomes fixed while their causes vary is not the counterfactual one.

**Path-dependence.** Select the new world from the old: the world of the extended series is the closest $B$-world to $s(A, @)$ on a backtracking ordering that holds the old world's effects fixed. That passes the test. But the world is no longer fixed from actuality, so this is not the PRP either. It also makes the open details of a finished work depend on the order in which its parts were released, and lets an earlier arbitrary selection, which no judgement tracks, set the coin.

Supervaluating over admissible selection functions, an option B&H mention, following Stalnaker [-@Stalnaker1980], and reject for themselves (185), and which Khoo [-@Khoo2026, §4] develops for fiction, abandons the single world. It passes the test only if every admissible selection keeps the landing fixed while the gust varies, which is the defaults view imposed as a penumbral constraint.

Each survivor is a selection rule for fiction that counterfactuals reject. That is the precise sense in which fiction is not counterfactual. B&H's reason to identify the two was the counterfactual parallel, and @sec-states shows that the parallel is predicted without the identification.

So the live single-world views are the three just described. Compare any of them with the story state.
- *Shared.* Both need the priors $\pi_w$. On the single-world side they enter through the chance–selection link.
- *Single world.* Adds a default world, an anchoring rule or a selection path, which no one could know and no judgement tracks. In return it gets classical logic for the fiction operator and bivalence for every bare claim.
- *Story state.* Adds gaps, governed by the logic of homogeneity, and two truth notions: transparent internal truth and assessment-sensitive rightness.
- *Data.* By absorption and the test, both predict the attitudes, the embedding patterns and the strengthening judgements.

B&H put the choice this way. Their argument, they say, is "fundamentally conditional in nature: if we are not systematically mistaken in our judgments about the kinds of attitudes that are appropriate to take toward indeterminate fictional claims, then there must be facts of the matter about any meaningful question one can ask about what's true in a work of fiction—facts whose grounds will in many cases be almost entirely arbitrary" (188). I grant the antecedent. Unlike Oppy and Raivars [-@OppyRaivars2026] and Khoo [-@Khoo2026], I accept B&H's judgements. The story state shows that the conditional is false: the judgements are explained without the facts. The facts no longer earn their keep as a unification with counterfactuals either. What remains is bivalence for its own sake, bought with arbitrary and unknowable facts that no judgement tracks. B&H's argument for the single world was abductive (182–183), and by the abductive standard it is now unsupported.

# Objections {#sec-objections}

**Isn't this just the standard analysis?** No. The standard analysis also lets a story's truths grow monotonically, and it gets (B) and (C) right. But it gets (A) and (D) wrong. Without the special the story settles nothing about the coin, so on the standard analysis "the coin would have landed heads" is false wherever the counterfactual takes us, and the credence in (D) is 0. Likewise the story does not settle what would have happened without the gust, so the credence in (A) is 0. The .5s come from the priors. The standard analysis is right about truth and wrong about credence. The story state keeps its view of truth and adds a Reality Principle for credence.

**Viewers will think the makers decided.** A reunion special that withholds an outcome invites the thought that someone knows the answer. If viewers judge (B) false because they think the makers decided, the judgement supports neither view. The stipulation that the makers have no view, and the probe proposed in @sec-test, address this. The real case also shows how strong the pull is. Recaps of the 2019 sequel treated it as revealing an answer the makers held. That is a datum about how viewers construe makers, not about what an undecided story makes true.

**Does the test tell against Lewis too?** Lewis's analyses also use counterfactuals, but variably strict ones [@Lewis1978]. On them what is true in a story is what holds at all the closest worlds where it is told as known fact, so no single world is selected. A detail that some of those worlds already satisfy leaves the story's truths in place. The test tells against the Stalnakerian identification, not against Lewis's, though Lewis's analyses, like the standard analysis, still need the priors to get the credences right.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

B&H showed that the standard analysis, with the attitude equivalence it validates, mispredicts our attitudes toward fictional indeterminacy. They were right about that. They then made two further moves. They took the attitudes as evidence of hidden facts, and they took counterfactuals to locate those facts. The first fails because the attitudes, and the embedding patterns, are equally well explained by a story state weighted by a Reality Principle for credence. The second fails because stories and counterfactuals respond differently to added detail. A detail that bears on an open chancy question can change the answer to a counterfactual. In a story it cannot, because the story never gave an answer to change.

Three things follow. Nothing makes it true that Holmes had an odd number of hairs when he met Watson. The identification of fictional truth with Stalnakerian counterfactual truth is false. And our graded attitudes to what stories leave open answer to a Reality Principle for credence, not to hidden facts.
